title: AWS Organizations
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of aws organizations and its relationship to AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to aws organizations.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn aws organizations in the context of AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: AWS Organizations matters because it is one part of aws security, governance and compliance. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 15: AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 15, AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 15 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** AWS Organizations belongs to AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance. Security is a lifecycle: identities, data protection, detection, governance, audit and incident response. Controls should be scoped, observable and tested rather than assumed from service defaults.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Organization structure; Management and member accounts; Organizational units; Delegated administration. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For aws organizations, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Organization structure
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Management and member accounts
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Organizational units
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: Delegated administration
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Security review checklist: AWS Organizations
content_blocks.code:
{
  "identity": "least privilege + MFA/federation",
  "data": "classification + encryption + retention",
  "network": "minimal exposure + private paths where appropriate",
  "detection": "audit events + threat findings + response owner",
  "evidence": "control owner + timestamp + follow-up"
}
content_blocks.expected_output: A review record that links controls to evidence and accountable follow-up; it is not itself a compliance certification.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “AWS Organizations”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for AWS Organizations with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: AWS Organizations is taught as part of AWS Security, Governance, and Compliance.
Security is a lifecycle: identities, data protection, detection, governance, audit and incident response. Controls should be scoped, observable and tested rather than assumed from service defaults.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
